Project 1 of 4 · Quant research · Solo · 2026

Stress-testing trading strategies until only one survived

I led a study of trading ideas on 10 years of real stock prices. The survivor, a risk-controlled reversal strategy, earned a Sharpe ratio of 0.44 (return per unit of risk) with a worst drop of 16.8%, half the S&P 500's, but returned less than the index.

Objective Test whether a small account can capture a well-documented market pattern too small for large funds, the way a quant researcher would: a literature hypothesis, a realistic backtest, true out-of-sample validation, and honest reporting of what failed.

0.44Out-of-sample Sharpe, after costs
−16.8%Max drawdown (S&P 500: −33.7%)
37Walk-forward test windows, 9+ years
29Unit tests guarding the pipeline

My contribution

Research lead: set the goals and pass bars, signed off on every stage

  • Set the goal: a strategy a small account could run, tested the way a quant researcher would before risking money.
  • Directed an AI coding agent (Claude Code) to build the pipeline: cleaning, a realistic backtest, walk-forward tests, a risk overlay.
  • Directed four follow-up studies, from volatility filters to ML signal searches; a library survey caught a wrong Sortino formula.
  • Set the bar the ML search had to clear, before it ran.
  • Signed off on each stage through three pull requests, backed by 29 unit tests.
  • Python
  • pandas
  • scikit-learn
  • PyTorch
  • statsmodels
  • Walk-forward validation
  • Permutation testing
  • Unit testing
  • Data cleaning

Against the objective

  • ✓Met Literature-based idea held up out of sample
  • ✓Met, with limits Realistic backtest (flat costs, survivorship bias)
  • Partly Out-of-sample test: probabilistic Sharpe 0.91, short of 0.95
  • ✓Met Honest reporting: every failed idea documented
  • ○Not met Beating the market (SPY Sharpe 0.85)

Constraints

Team: Solo · Timeline: Sep 19 to 20, 2026 · Capital: Sized for a few thousand dollars; no leverage · Data: Free public prices (Yahoo Finance) · Costs: 10 bps (0.10%) per trade, likely optimistic

What I learned

One good number is not evidence. A filter that scored 0.32 at one lookback flipped to −0.06 at another, so I now check results across settings.

Project 2 of 4 · Client analytics · Consult Your Community · 2025

A donor dashboard that shows a crime victim nonprofit which donors come back

I analyzed Crime Victim Center (CVC) donor records, found that a small group of donors gave most of the dollars, and built a five-page Streamlit dashboard that repeats that check, plus retention, map and campaign views, on each new GiveButter export. It fully covers the brief's donor-ranking goal and partly covers segmentation, tracking and outreach.

Objective CVC's brief asked for a donor strategy aimed at high-value and monthly donors. Five of its goals depend on donor data; I rate each under “Against the objective.”

Project 3 of 4 · Instrumentation · Team of 2 · 2026

Turning 10,000 noisy sweeps into a working diamond magnetic-field sensor

I built the Python pipeline behind a diamond-based magnetic-field sensor. It drives the instruments, captures 10,000 sweeps, rejects glitched ones and fits every spectrum: up to 8 resonance lines, R² ≥ 0.97 in all 10 conditions. Readings ran below the coil's predicted field; one constant 0.61 mT offset, fitted afterward and consistent with stray magnetization, brings 0.4 to 0.8 A within about 1.1σ of theory.

Objective Build a magnetic-field sensor from teaching-lab hardware and test it against the coil's predicted field. Defects in diamond (NV centers) glow red under a green laser and dim by a few percent at a microwave resonance near 2.9 GHz; a magnetic field splits that resonance, and the split gives the field.

10,000Sweeps captured (10 currents × 1,000)
85%Kept after automated QC (8,517)
≥ 0.97Fit R² in every condition
1.1σLargest gap to coil theory at 0.4–0.8 A, after one fitted offset

My contribution

Built all software; sole committer on the repo

  • Automated an oscilloscope and a function generator from Python (PyVISA/SCPI): 1,000 sweeps per condition.
  • Engineered QC that rejects glitched sweeps with a data-derived threshold (85% kept).
  • Diagnosed a trigger that never locked and fixed its root cause; fixed a jagged frequency axis and a sign bug.
  • Designed an adaptive fit that counts dips first; per-line depths lifted R² at 0.5 A from 0.88 to 0.99.
  • Propagated uncertainty into every field reading and the theory band.
  • Paired with an AI assistant (Claude Code) on the code and docs; documented it all: README, uncertainty write-up, lab notebook, paper draft.
  • Python
  • PyVISA / SCPI
  • NumPy
  • SciPy
  • matplotlib
  • Signal processing
  • Data QC
  • Nonlinear fitting
  • Uncertainty analysis

Against the objective

  • ✓Met Clean without distorting: the data-derived threshold reproduced my hand-tuned split
  • ✓Met Detect the resonance: a 7.48% dip, close to the roughly 8% in the literature
  • ✓Met Resolve the splitting: up to 8 lines, every fit R² ≥ 0.97
  • Partly Match coil theory: readings ran low; one 0.61 mT offset fits the gap, and 0.3 A stays a 3.1σ outlier

Constraints

Team: 2 people; I built all the software · Timeline: 7 lab sessions, analysis done by Sep 22 · Context: Advanced undergraduate physics lab course, fall 2026 · Starting point: A LabVIEW design and two- and four-dip fit models (one shared depth) from the lab handout · Data volume: Captures up to several GB, past GitHub's 100 MB file limit

What I learned

Build tools that make problems visible. QC plots and a read-only instrument check found most fixes; full coil geometry cut the gap from about 30σ to 3 to 13σ.

Project 4 of 4 · Neuroaesthetics research · WashU · 2025

Measuring why people like mosaic art: a benchmarked 982-image feature pipeline

I wrote the MATLAB feature extractor for a WashU study of why people like mosaics: 982 mosaics into 172 features each. Benchmarked against a published study, it reproduces the original's average color and brightness measures (9 of 18 global features at |r| ≥ 0.7), not yet its hue-count, blur or segment-shape features. On 70 pilot images, the team ranked features against ratings with my table.

Objective A 2021 study predicted people's ratings of paintings from simple and complex visual features. Does that hold for mosaics? My piece: turn every image into numbers a regression can use, benchmarked against the published baseline.

982Mosaic images in the feature table (979 extracted cleanly)
172Features per image
23 / 83Published-study features my statistics match (30 re-running its code)
70 × 5Pilot images × ratings each

My contribution

Undergraduate researcher; image feature extraction and benchmarking

  • Revived the original study's MATLAB code on Windows: rebuilt its C++ binaries and checked outputs against stored values.
  • Engineered a new extractor: 18 statistics on 9 color channels plus FFT spectral centroids, reusing the original's hue-harmony models.
  • Benchmarked it against the original 83 features: 23 matched on my first pass, 30 with its hue and region code ported.
  • Diagnosed randomness in the hue-model choice (2 of 100 repeat runs changed) and in graph-cut segments.
  • Evaluated graph cuts and SAM2 for tile-level features; prototyped HOG features for tile flow.
  • Delivered the feature table for our pilot analysis; co-authored the symposium poster and abstract.

  • ○Not yet The original's hue-count, blur and segment-shape features
  • Preliminary Pilot (70 images) ranks candidate features; no model validated yet

Constraints

Team: 9 on the roster, led by Prof. Ralf Wessel; I built low-level features with Prady Sepulveda · Ratings cost: ~$10 per participant-hour on Prolific (team estimate); pilot: 350 ratings · Tooling: Legacy MATLAB/C++ code built for macOS, rebuilt for Windows; no labeled data for deep models

What I learned

Validation before modeling. Rebuilding legacy code, matching it feature by feature and chasing randomness is how I know which parts of the table to trust.
